messages.body_plain:
Mike

I can't duplicate your problem using package versions 1.0.1 for Distance  and 2.2.2 for mrds

library(Distance)
data("capercaillie")
conversion.factor <- convert_units("meter", "kilometer", "hectare")
bins <- c(0, seq(from=7.5, to=67.5, by=10), 80)
bins
caper.hn.bin <- ds(data=capercaillie, key="hn", adjustment="cos", cutpoints=bins,
                   convert.units=conversion.factor)
caper.hn.bin$ddf$meta.data$binned
gof_ds(caper.hn.bin)

What am I not doing that you are doing?  Are we working with similar versions?

Eric Rexstad
Senior Research Fellow, CREEM, Univ. of St Andrews, Charity SC013532
eric.r...@st-andrews.ac.uk
The Observatory, Buchanan Gardens, St Andrews KY16 9LZ

Thanks for the super quick response Eric, much appreciated. I am using the same package versions as you.

 However I differ in that am attempting to fit a detection function using ddf to some ESAS (seabird) data as an initial part of a dsm analysis. This data is binned into 4 distance bins.

See code below -
head(gu)

6       1        50     100    1        2 597.6238 [m] 2019-6-T9-22
7       2       100     200    1        2 597.6238 [m] 2019-6-T9-22
8       3        50     100    1        2 597.6238 [m] 2019-6-T9-22

12      6        50     100    1        1 597.6238 [m] 2019-6-T9-11

gu.hn.null <- ddf(dsmodel=~mcds(key="hn", formula=~1),
              data = gu, method="ds",
              meta.data=list(width=300, binned=T, breaks = c(0,50,100,200,300)))

gof_ds(gu.hn.null)

messages.body_plain:
Mike

I don't spend much time using mrds these days, so I'm fuzzy on its workings.  But if you use ddf() for model fitting, rather than ds(), seems you ought to perform your goodness-of-fit testing with ddf.gof() rather than with gof_ds()

See if that pairing makes things better.

Eric Rexstad
Senior Research Fellow, CREEM, Univ. of St Andrews, Charity SC013532

eric.r...@st-andrews.ac.uk

The Observatory, Buchanan Gardens, St Andrews KY16 9LZ

Thanks again for your time Eric. ddf.gof certainly produces a result. See below.

I had tried this previously but was really looking to produce a detection function plot overlain on my binned distance data to visually assess, as I thought gof_ds did (think i have this wrong....)

ddf.gof(gu.hn.null,  breaks = c(0,50,100,200,300),
+                       main="GU goodness of fit")

Goodness of fit results for ddf object

Observed  734.00000 724.00000 589.00000  386.0000 2433.0000
Expected  692.41886 612.81428 812.76253  315.0043 2433.0000
Chisquare   2.49703  20.17294  61.60431   16.0010  100.2753

P = 0 with 2 degrees of freedom

Mike

Working with binned data, you won't get a visualisation of fit from ddf.gof() as it will only create qq-plots, and those are only available with exact distance data.  You should get a visualisation from simply calling plot(gu.hn.null)

Eric Rexstad
Senior Research Fellow, CREEM, Univ. of St Andrews, Charity SC013532
eric.r...@st-andrews.ac.uk
The Observatory, Buchanan Gardens, St Andrews KY16 9LZ

messages.subject: Distance 7.3 Release 2
messages.subject_clean: Distance 7.3 Release 2
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance for Windows users,

We are pleased to announce an update to our Distance for Windows
software: Distance 7.3 Release 2.  The new release updates the R
packages used by the MRDS, DSM and MA analysis engines, and the
simulation engine, with bug fixes and compatibility with R 4.0.  If you
use any of these engines, we recommend you download the new release.
More information about what is in the updated R packages is given below.

With best wishes,

Len Thomas, Distance Development Group, University of St Andrews

More information:

The new release contains versions of the mrds, dsm, mads and DSsim
packages, which were compiled under R 4.0.2.  They implement the
following changes:

mrds 2.2.2
----------

* fix issue in predict() when uniform key functions are used with new data.
* new function p_dist_table() to show the distribution of estimated
probabilities of detection. Useful for covariate models to determine
issues with very small ps.
* new function add_df_covar_line(), which can be used to add lines plots
showing the detection function for a given covariate combination. Thanks
to various members of the distance sampling mailing list for this
suggestion.
* plots produced by
plot.ds/plot.rem/plot.rem.fi/plot.trial/plot.trial.fi/plot.io/plot.io.fi/plot.det.tables <http://plot.rem.fi/plot.trial/plot.trial.fi/plot.io/plot.io.fi/plot.det.tables>
now use same defaults as R 4.0.0 ("lightgrey" bars for histograms). Some
deprecated arguments to plot.ds were removed.

mrds 2.2.1
----------

* hessian now returned when solnp (constrained optimisation) is used to
fit the detection function
* Check for NA covariate values, thanks to Ana Cañadas for highlighting
this issue.
* enable P2 variance estimator for points
* Corrected handling of NA covariates
* new option se.fit for predict.ds to obtain standard errors for the
probability of detection or ESW
* Fixed a bug in dht when left truncation is used. Previously left
truncation was ignored. See
https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/mrds/issues/22 thanks to Carl
Schwarz for finding this bug.
* Fix bug where two objects could have a missing observer and no error
was thrown. Thanks to Ainars Aunins for reporting this bug and Eric
Rexstad for diagnosing.

dsm 2.3.1
---------

  * transect type (line or point) is now determined from the detection
function rather than using the transect= argument
  * multiple detection functions are now possible, use a list() of
fitted detection functions supplied to ddf.obj= argument to dsm().
dsm.var.gam, dsm.var.prop and dsm_varprop are compatible. Vignette
coming soon. Thanks to Dave Fifield and Ewan Wakefield for extensive
testing and suggestions.
  * strip transects now handled using the dummy_ddf() function.

dsm 2.3.0
---------

  * fixed dsm_varprop (gam.fixed.priors) for response distributions with
fixed scale parameters. Negative binomial results before now may have
been incorrect!

dsm 2.2.18
----------

  * Clarification of the predict.dsm return documentation. Thanks to
Dave Fifield for the suggestion.
  * off.set=NULL lead to predictions of 0 when density was used. Now
just returns density. Thanks to Dave Fifield for the catch.

dsm 2.2.17
----------

  * Now Suggests package "sp" (needed for some parts of the mexdolphin
example data)

mads 0.1.6
----------

New Features

   * Added % complete progress counter

Bug Fixes

   * Fixed example dataset

DSsim 1.1.5
-----------

Bug fixes

   * Fixed warnings bug generated when there were too few data points
   * Code to calculate perpendicular distance is more robust
   * Fixed incorrect true expected cluster size values in simulation summary
   * Documentation corrections

DSsim 1.1.4
-----------

New Features

   * Can now generate equal spaced zigzag designs with any design axis
angle and can generate two sets of complimentary zigzags.
   * User can now select between using all repetitions where at least
one model converged and ony repetitions where all models convgered. This
is selected when calling summary on a simulation object.
   * Now tells user which models cause issued in mrds.

Bug Fixes
   * Improved backwards compatibility, including updating the S4 objects
to include default values for missing slots.

--
Len Thomas  len.t...@st-andrews.ac.uk  lenthomas.org <http://lenthomas.org>  @len_thom
Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
and School of Mathematics and Statistics
The Observatory, University of St Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ
Office: UK+1334-461801  Admin: UK+1334-461842

The University of St Andrews is a charity
registered in Scotland, No SC013532.

messages.subject: Full geographic stratification Vs.using stratum as a covariate ~ some mysterious results..
messages.subject_clean: Full geographic stratification Vs.using stratum as a covariate ~ some mysterious results..
messages.body_plain:
Hi All!

I am conducting analysis
on line transect data from a stratified study region (2 PAs), one species, one
year. I require abundance estimates per region (i.e. stratum).

Following this
vignette: http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.html
in R, I compared (1) full geographic stratification, (2) using stratum as a
covariate, and (3) a pooled detection function shared between data. The 2
strata have similar effort and size. Observations # are 57 for 1 stratum and 49
for the other. I use the same key function (no adjustments) and truncation distance
for all model comparisons and tried both half-normal (HN) and hazard-rate (HR).

Based on original
data exploration, I had reason to believe detection functions could be
different between PAs, and as there are some differences in habitat and relief
(though not major) there is some ecological foundation for this as well.

The AIC score was
slightly lower for the fully stratified HN model (summed) compared to the
pooled HN model (delta AIC 1.5). But when comparing the stratum-specific
abundances, (following the case study described in Buckland et al. 2001
pp.71-74), it appeared that they were biased for the pooled model by ~15%. This
tempts me to discard the pooled model.

Interestingly,
the MCDS-HN model produced the exact same AIC and abundance
estimates with a very slight difference in lcl and ucl (only 1 individual on a
population of ~3,000) as the stratified CDS-HN models. The MCDS-HR model did
produce different outputs when compared to the stratified CDS-HR. HN models
haves lower AICs compared to HR models (delta AIC 2-3). I triple checked my
codes and re-ran with different data subsets & truncation distances, and
the same things happens.

Based on all the
above, my questions are:

1.)    How is it possible the abundance & AIC are
so identical using methods (1) versus (2), and only for HN but not HR? Is there
a fundamental concept that I am missing here?

2.)    What is wisdom? Is there a strong argument for
choosing one of the analytical methods over the other? I know in this case the
results are the same but ignoring that, would there be a reason to justify MCDS
is a better approach compared to CDS o vice versa given the conditions outlined
above?

3.)    Is it in general preferable to apply MCDS when
sample size per stratum is low (in this case below 60-80 for each but close)?
Is the required minimum sample size different when using your stratum as
covariate and “full” stratum, versus “full” stratum only?

4.)    I have the possibility to combine this dataset
with those of previous year(s), adding to the sample size but possibly creating
bias. My aim is to use year-region specific estimates that can be compared
between years to monitor trends. I am not very happy with the detection
function and histogram of one of the strata using just this years’ data (it’s
shows some weird gaps and peaks that are not explained by rounding/heaping),
and thought that perhaps adding data from other years could smooth out these
artifacts.

I really tried to
be as short as I could, but didn’t manage very well. Apologies! And thank you
so much in advance for your help! Mylo

messages.body_plain:
Mylo

Thanks for your question and your astute observation regarding identical estimates derived from full stratification and strata as covariate in conjunction with the half normal key function.

I can conform your findings using the minke data set included in the Distance  package:

library(Distance)
data(minke)
hn.full.N <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="North",], key="hn", truncation=1.5)
hn.full.S <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="South",], key="hn", truncation=1.5)
hn.cov <- ds(data=minke, key="hn",truncation = 1.5, formula = ~Region.Label)
all.equal(hn.full.N$ddf$criterion + hn.full.S$ddf$criterion,hn.cov$ddf$criterion)
hn.cov$dht$individuals$N
hn.full.N$dht$individuals$N
hn.full.S$dht$individuals$N

hr.full.N <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="North",], key="hr", truncation=1.5)
hr.full.S <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="South",], key="hr", truncation=1.5)
hr.cov <- ds(data=minke, key="hr",truncation = 1.5, formula = ~Region.Label)
all.equal(hr.full.N$ddf$criterion + hr.full.S$ddf$criterion,hr.cov$ddf$criterion)
hr.cov$dht$individuals$N
hr.full.N$dht$individuals$N
hr.full.S$dht$individuals$N

The equivalence for the half normal key function is exact, which the equivalence in abundance estimates for the hazard rate key function is close, but not exact.

I'm afraid I do not have an explanation for this behaviour.  I don't know of a reason why this should be the case.  Perhaps someone else more clever has an explanation.

Regarding general advice about producing stratum-specific estimates.  Employing a covariate in the detection function provides you with confidence you are using stratum-specific detection functions to produce stratum-specific estimates.  The only down-side would be when the two strata have equivalent detection functions, you would be estimating an additional parameter in the detection function causing some reduction in the precision of the resulting estimates.

When using full stratum-specific estimates (with stratum specific detection functions), the number of detections in each stratum need to be sufficient such that the detection function in each stratum stands on its own; meaning the advice of Buckland et al. (2001) of 60-80 detections would be necessary per stratum.  I can offer no clear guidance on the number of detections per stratum when using stratum as a covariate.

Regarding your item (4).  Be careful when pooling data across years to assess temporal trends.  Pooling data induces a dependence between estimates.  This dependence is dampened through the use of year as a covariate.

Covariates in lieu of full stratification is discussed in the context of "species as strata" in the vignette: http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-spec-covar/species-covariate-distill.html

Eric Rexstad
Senior Research Fellow, CREEM, Univ. of St Andrews, Charity SC013532
eric.r...@st-andrews.ac.uk
The Observatory, Buchanan Gardens, St Andrews KY16 9LZ

messages.body_plain:
I think the reason is that the half-normal has a scale parameter only, and with the scale parameter being estimated separately for each stratum, you get the same result as a stratified analysis.  The hazard-rate model also has a shape parameter, and if the shape parameter is estimated independently for each stratum, you’ll get a different answer than if you use MCDS, which allows only the scale parameter to differ between strata.

Steve Buckland

all.equal(hn.full.N$ddf$criterion + hn.full.S$ddf$criterion,hn.cov$ddf$criterion)

hn.cov$dht$individuals$N

hn.full.N$dht$individuals$N

hn.full.S$dht$individuals$N

hr.full.N <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="North",], key="hr", truncation=1.5)

hr.full.S <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="South",], key="hr", truncation=1.5)

hr.cov <- ds(data=minke, key="hr",truncation = 1.5, formula = ~Region.Label)

all.equal(hr.full.N$ddf$criterion + hr.full.S$ddf$criterion,hr.cov$ddf$criterion)

hr.cov$dht$individuals$N

hr.full.N$dht$individuals$N

hr.full.S$dht$individuals$N

The equivalence for the half normal key function is exact, which the equivalence in abundance estimates for the hazard rate key function is close, but not exact.

I'm afraid I do not have an explanation for this behaviour.  I don't know of a reason why this should be the case.  Perhaps someone else more clever has an explanation.

Regarding general advice about producing stratum-specific estimates.  Employing a covariate in the detection function provides you with confidence you are using stratum-specific detection functions to produce stratum-specific estimates.  The only down-side would be when the two strata have equivalent detection functions, you would be estimating an additional parameter in the detection function causing some reduction in the precision of the resulting estimates.

When using full stratum-specific estimates (with stratum specific detection functions), the number of detections in each stratum need to be sufficient such that the detection function in each stratum stands on its own; meaning the advice of Buckland et al. (2001) of 60-80 detections would be necessary per stratum.  I can offer no clear guidance on the number of detections per stratum when using stratum as a covariate.

Regarding your item (4).  Be careful when pooling data across years to assess temporal trends.  Pooling data induces a dependence between estimates.  This dependence is dampened through the use of year as a covariate.

Covariates in lieu of full stratification is discussed in the context of "species as strata" in the vignette:  http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-spec-covar/species-covariate-distill.html

Eric Rexstad

> Hi All!

>
> I am conducting analysis on line transect data from a stratified study region (2 PAs), one species, one year. I require abundance estimates per region (i.e. stratum).
>
>
>
> Following this vignette:  http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.html in R, I compared (1) full geographic stratification, (2) using stratum as a covariate, and (3) a pooled detection function shared between data. >
>
>

>
>
>

But when comparing the stratum-specific abundances, (following the case study described in Buckland et al. 2001 pp.71-74), it appeared that they were biased for the pooled model by ~15%. This tempts me to discard the pooled model.
>
>
>
> Interestingly, the MCDS-HN model produced the exact same AIC and abundance estimates with a very slight difference in lcl and ucl (only 1 individual on a population of ~3,000) as the stratified CDS-HN models. >
>

>
>
>

>
>
>
> 2.)    What is wisdom? Is there a strong argument for choosing one of the analytical methods over the other? >
>
>

>
>

My aim is to use year-region specific estimates that can be compared between years to monitor trends. I am not very happy with the detection function and histogram of one of the strata using just this years’ data (it’s shows some weird gaps and peaks that are not explained by rounding/heaping), and thought that perhaps adding data from other years could smooth out these artifacts.
>
>
>

> >

Measuring distances to "resting" animals caused problems in simulations, because an animal that remains in front of the camera can contribute large numbers of observations, and if they are at moderate to far distances, decreasing functions may not fit the data well. > > > > > > > > > Scott, regarding your question: "How are the snapshot moments defined/quantified": You define them as specific times of day. You also chose a daily time interval or intervals during which you will measure distances if animals are detected.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > It's helpful to plot detection times over the 24-hour day before measuring distances, because you might decide to reduce your daily survey duration to e.g. near dawn and dusk for crepuscular species or daylight hours for diurnal species (as in our article), and there's no need to measure distances to animals detected outside of this interval.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Also choose a value for t (duration of time step between snapshot moments). If t = 3, you could define moments as e.g. 0, 3, 6..., 57 seconds after the even minute, OR as 2, 5, 8,..., etc. seconds after the even minute, in real time. Moments are the same for all cameras. Regardless of when a camera is triggered, distances are measured only at these moments.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Tk is the total number of seconds a camera operates at location k. It's convenient to define a daily Tk, in seconds. This is the "time interval during which you will measure distances" above, so it might be less than the number of seconds in 24 hours; it might be the number of seconds within a 2- or 12-hour period. Multiply this by the number of days a camera operated and could have detected animals at a location to obtain Tk at that location. Then, dividing Tk by t (both in seconds) gives you the total number of opportunities to detect an animal at a location over the duration of a survey. This is your temporal effort at that location. Enter it as "Effort" in software IFF you are quantifying spatial effort < than a circle using a multiplier or the sampling_fraction argument. Alternatively, you can avoid multipliers and calculate Effort as described in the article (incorporating both spatial and temporal components)..
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Note that if we detected one animal at every opportunity, the encounter rate would be 1.0. In practice, encounter rates (detections per opportunity) are very low with camera trap point transects, because we observe no animals during most opportunities.

> > > > > > > > > > > Also choose a value for t (duration of time step between snapshot moments). If t = 3, you could define moments as e.g. 0, 3, 6..., 57 seconds after the even minute, OR as 2, 5, 8,..., etc. seconds after the even minute, in real time. Moments are the same for all cameras. Regardless of when a camera is triggered, distances are measured only at these moments.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Tk is the total number of seconds a camera operates at location k. It's convenient to define a daily Tk, in seconds. This is the "time interval during which you will measure distances" above, so it might be less than the number of seconds in 24 hours; it might be the number of seconds within a 2- or 12-hour period. Multiply this by the number of days a camera operated and could have detected animals at a location to obtain Tk at that location. Then, dividing Tk by t (both in seconds) gives you the total number of opportunities to detect an animal at a location over the duration of a survey. This is your temporal effort at that location. Enter it as "Effort" in software IFF you are quantifying spatial effort < than a circle using a multiplier or the sampling_fraction argument. Alternatively, you can avoid multipliers and calculate Effort as described in the article (incorporating both spatial and temporal components)..
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Note that if we detected one animal at every opportunity, the encounter rate would be 1.0. In practice, encounter rates (detections per opportunity) are very low with camera trap point transects, because we observe no animals during most opportunities.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Hope this helps,
> > > > > > > > > > > Eric H

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Using dsm.var.prop
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jez, hi listfolk,

You might find this slide (and the following 4 or so) useful in this
situation:

http://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-dsm-2020/slides/dsm1-refresher-what_is_a_dsm.html#40

The basic rule is:

count can only be used when covariates only vary between segments/points
(not within). dsm.var.prop can only be used with count.

abundance.est/density.est can be used in any situation but must assume
independence and therefore use the delta method, as implemented in
dsm.var.gam.

I'll try to clear up the documentation to be more consistent between
pages for our next release.

best,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
If the burst settings were such that if any of images fell on one of the pre-defined intervals (e.g. :00, :02, :04 etc of each minute), then you would use each of those that fell on one of those intervals as a detection (snapshot) and measure distance.

This could occur if your camera sensor's recovery time is greater than the chosen CTDS interval period divided by the number of images per burst. In your case,  X second periods / 3 photos. If you are using the typical 2s period, then 2/3 = 0.67 seconds. If your camera trap sensor's recovery time during bursts is greater than 0.67, then it would be possible for 2 photos taken in a single 3-photo burst to be used as two independent snapshots. This is pretty slow for a modern camera trap, but if you took more photos per burst, you are more likely to overlap multiple snapshot moments (e.g. 10 image burst, t = 2s, then 2/10 = 0.2s which is a pretty quick recovery time).

Snapshot moments are independent of the trigger moment, if I understand correctly. This is why video is sometimes used - the sensor is triggered at 14:21:17, video recorded for 15 seconds, then snapshots at e.g. 14:21:18, 14:21:20, 14:21:22, and 14:21:24 are selected from that video, with the animal leaving the field of view at 14:21:25. In this example, you would have pre-defined your 't' interval to be 2s. With a photo based approach, you would set the camera to take enough images that one falls close to each of these pre-defined moments during the period the animal is in front of the sensor (ignoring resting/avoidance/curiosity for the moment for simplicity).

Please let me know if I'm mistaken here - I have yet to implement our survey but will be basing our design on the assumptions above! We intend to use photos rather than videos for data management and processing reasons.

messages.subject_clean: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling with camera traps - vignettes or training courses?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Scott,

According to the original article, snapshot moments should be independent of triggering times, and predetermined as specific times of day. E.g. 0, 2, 4, ...., 58 seconds after the even minute for and interval (t ) = 2 seconds. In practice, we might look at our data after they had been collected and decide to set the interval to 1 or 3 or more seconds (to avoid missed detections, or unnecessary work), but we would still measure distances at those specific moments... Also, we would often measure distances to an animal or animals multiple times as it or they pass through the field of view (whenever it/they moves slowly enough to be present in the field of view during > 1 snapshot moment). We recommended programming cameras to record either video or long, rapid, bursts of still images, to ensure that some images would align (almost) perfectly with snapshot moments.

I know there has been some discussion about how to collect data when cameras are not programmed to record e.g. video. With small t and cameras that can be triggered again immediately after recording an image, bias induced by the fact that observations of distance are not independent of trigger times should be slight. This approach would require small t  (not sure how small, but probably no longer than 2 seconds, and ideally shorter) so that observed distances would describe the animals' path through the zone of potential detection, not the location upon initial detection, which is expected to yield a positively biased distribution of observed distances. Multiple observations of distance to slow-moving animals would be recorded during a single pass through the zone of potential detection.

Regarding your specific question, I think whether or not your 3 images would be recorded as one or as 2 or 3 observations depends on what t has been set to, and how far apart in time those 3 images are in time. E.g. if t = 2 and the images are 1 second apart, we would measure distances to animals in the first and third image. If t = 1 and the images are 2 seconds apart, we would miss detections at half of our snapshot moments, causing severe negative bias. You would only treat 3 images as one observation of distance if the time elapsed between images was much less than t.

Eric H

The estimates do fit well with known densities elsewhere on Guam. One problem is that the cameras were in place before the fence was put up. > > > Good day Scott,
> > >
> > > As Eric and Steve mention, we accept and include non-independent observations. If its midpoint is visible, and the time is within Tk and during a snapshot moment, we record distance and include the observations. It doesn't cause cause bias because a single animal can only be detected once per location per snapshot moment.
> > >
> > > The issue with apparent heaping is potentially more complicated. Measuring distances to "resting" animals caused problems in simulations, because an animal that remains in front of the camera can contribute large numbers of observations, and if they are at moderate to far distances, decreasing functions may not fit the data well. Our (imperfect) solution was to avoid sampling during times when animals "rest".
> > >
> > > Animals that are awake and moving slightly (thus triggering the sensor) but not going anywhere could cause the same effect, and we don't have a clear reason to sensor the observations (the animal is "active").
> > >
> > > I would suggest checking the times of day when cameras detected these lingering animals, and see if they are similar. If there are specific times of day when animals are at their most mobile (e.g. crepuscular?), such that animals detected at these times pass by the camera (often contributing > 1, but not dozens or hundreds, of observations) rather than lingering in front of it, then you could limit Tk to these times. That could exclude most or all lingering animals from the data, improving fit without causing bias.
> > >

> > >
> > > If you had only one animal that lingered in front of a camera and this animal created a "bump" in the observed distances far from 0, you could just say so and exclude the animal or most of the observations it contributed.
> > >

> > > > > > > > > > Good day Scott, and thanks Eric and Steve,
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Scott, regarding your question: "How are the snapshot moments defined/quantified": You define them as specific times of day. You also chose a daily time interval or intervals during which you will measure distances if animals are detected.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > It's helpful to plot detection times over the 24-hour day before measuring distances, because you might decide to reduce your daily survey duration to e.g. near dawn and dusk for crepuscular species or daylight hours for diurnal species (as in our article), and there's no need to measure distances to animals detected outside of this interval.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Also choose a value for t (duration of time step between snapshot moments). Regardless of when a camera is triggered, distances are measured only at these moments.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Tk is the total number of seconds a camera operates at location k. It's convenient to define a daily Tk, in seconds. This is the "time interval during which you will measure distances" above, so it might be less than the number of seconds in 24 hours; it might be the number of seconds within a 2- or 12-hour period. Multiply this by the number of days a camera operated and could have detected animals at a location to obtain Tk at that location. Then, dividing Tk by t (both in seconds) gives you the total number of opportunities to detect an animal at a location over the duration of a survey. This is your temporal effort at that location. Enter it as "Effort" in software IFF you are quantifying spatial effort < than a circle using a multiplier or the sampling_fraction argument. Alternatively, you can avoid multipliers and calculate Effort as described in the article (incorporating both spatial and temporal components)..
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Note that if we detected one animal at every opportunity, the encounter rate would be 1.0. In practice, encounter rates (detections per opportunity) are very low with camera trap point transects, because we observe no animals during most opportunities.

messages.subject: Re: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling with camera traps - vignettes or training courses?
messages.subject_clean: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling with camera traps - vignettes or training courses?
messages.body_plain:
Here's a little graphic I made to help illustrate the method to our team, perhaps it would be useful. Here, we pre-selected a t of 2 seconds, and with the snapshot falling on :00, :02, :04  etc of every minute. This shows the images or frames we would select under 4 different setups - one video, and 3 photo mode setups with different recovery times and burst modes (depending on camera model). Here, an animal enters the sensor FOV at 08:01:12.8 and remains in view for about 12 seconds. Each sensor triggers, and following a short delay (trigger time, dotted orange) begins to capture video or bursts of images. From this data, we select either video frames or photos (red lines) that are closest to the snapshot time (blue lines). For the video mode, a continuous video is captured for a defined length of time. For the photo modes, images are recorded with each firing of the sensor. This  shows why a short recovery time (between bursts) is required for CTDS. If the recovery time (a.k.a interval) was set to 15 seconds, the sensor would only fire once during the animal's time in the FOV. By setting the interval low, or using a higher number of images in each burst, a more continuous coverage of images is captured, allowing you to select images that are closest to the snapshot moments, and reducing bias. You can also see here how a single trigger event can produce more than one capture, if the burst continues over two snapshot moments (or includes images that are the closest to two snapshot moments, even if they don't fully overlap).

On Monday, 13 July 2020 at 22:42:02 UTC+7 ej...@st-andrews.ac.uk wrote:
> Hi Scott,
>
> According to the original article, snapshot moments should be independent of triggering times, and predetermined as specific times of day. E.g. 0, 2, 4, ...., 58 seconds after the even minute for and interval (t ) = 2 seconds. In practice, we might look at our data after they had been collected and decide to set the interval to 1 or 3 or more seconds (to avoid missed detections, or unnecessary work), but we would still measure distances at those specific moments... Also, we would often measure distances to an animal or animals multiple times as it or they pass through the field of view (whenever it/they moves slowly enough to be present in the field of view during > 1 snapshot moment). We recommended programming cameras to record either video or long, rapid, bursts of still images, to ensure that some images would align (almost) perfectly with snapshot moments.
>
> I know there has been some discussion about how to collect data when cameras are not programmed to record e.g. video. With small t and cameras that can be triggered again immediately after recording an image, bias induced by the fact that observations of distance are not independent of trigger times should be slight. This approach would require small t  (not sure how small, but probably no longer than 2 seconds, and ideally shorter) so that observed distances would describe the animals' path through the zone of potential detection, not the location upon initial detection, which is expected to yield a positively biased distribution of observed distances. Multiple observations of distance to slow-moving animals would be recorded during a single pass through the zone of potential detection.
>
> Regarding your specific question, I think whether or not your 3 images would be recorded as one or as 2 or 3 observations depends on what t has been set to, and how far apart in time those 3 images are in time. E.g. if t = 2 and the images are 1 second apart, we would measure distances to animals in the first and third image. If t = 1 and the images are 2 seconds apart, we would miss detections at half of our snapshot moments, causing severe negative bias. You would only treat 3 images as one observation of distance if the time elapsed between images was much less than t.
>
> Eric H
>
> On Sunday, 12 July 2020 at 22:20:38 UTC-4 scott Vogt wrote:
> > Hello Again,
> >
> > Have another question. I think I know the answer but want to make sure. If our cameras are set to take 3 images automatically when triggered, then those 3 frames are all within the same  snapshot moment and would be counted as one detection and distance, correct?
> >
> > Scott
> >
> >
> > On Friday, June 19, 2020 at 7:35:10 AM UTC+10, scott Vogt wrote:
> > > Hello Eric,
> > >
> > > the substrate is limestone karst and is very rocky. I think the animals (deer and pigs) just move slowly because of that.
> > >
> > > I've been putting the distance data into bins of varying sizes and that has helped. This helps the model fit but the density estimates are not all that different from the models with bad fit. Six deer were recognizable as individuals as were three pigs. Extrapolating the percentage of known to unknown animals for a population estimate and using known home ranges (gps collars) for estimating the area sampled produced a very similar density estimate for the deer and a lower estimate for the pigs but still in the ballpark.
> > >
> > > The area is 35 ha and was just enclosed by fencing to keep out the deer and pigs. The area will be "de-ungulated" in the coming months so we'll be able to see how accurate the estimates are. The estimates do fit well with known densities elsewhere on Guam. One problem is that the cameras were in place before the fence was put up. Fence construction might have moved some animals off of the site. I don't think that happened but it's possible.
> > >
> > > Thank you very much everyone for all of the help!
> > >
> > > Scott
> > >
> > >
> > > On Thursday, June 18, 2020 at 12:19:24 AM UTC+10, Eric Howe wrote:
> > > > Good day Scott,
> > > >
> > > > As Eric and Steve mention, we accept and include non-independent observations. If its midpoint is visible, and the time is within Tk and during a snapshot moment, we record distance and include the observations. It doesn't cause cause bias because a single animal can only be detected once per location per snapshot moment.
> > > >
> > > > The issue with apparent heaping is potentially more complicated. Measuring distances to "resting" animals caused problems in simulations, because an animal that remains in front of the camera can contribute large numbers of observations, and if they are at moderate to far distances, decreasing functions may not fit the data well. Our (imperfect) solution was to avoid sampling during times when animals "rest".
> > > >
> > > > Animals that are awake and moving slightly (thus triggering the sensor) but not going anywhere could cause the same effect, and we don't have a clear reason to sensor the observations (the animal is "active").
> > > >
> > > > I would suggest checking the times of day when cameras detected these lingering animals, and see if they are similar. If there are specific times of day when animals are at their most mobile (e.g. crepuscular?), such that animals detected at these times pass by the camera (often contributing > 1, but not dozens or hundreds, of observations) rather than lingering in front of it, then you could limit Tk to these times. That could exclude most or all lingering animals from the data, improving fit without causing bias.
> > > >
> > > > Bessone et al. (2020) sensored observations of animals obviously reacting to the camera, and this improved fit (another imperfect solution to a similar problem).   https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2664.13602.
> > > >
> > > > If you had only one animal that lingered in front of a camera and this animal created a "bump" in the observed distances far from 0, you could just say so and exclude the animal or most of the observations it contributed.
> > > >
> > > > Eric
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, 16 June 2020 17:52:48 UTC-4, scott Vogt wrote:
> > > > > Well that didn't take long.
> > > > >
> > > > > if we have the same animal that lingers in the area over multiple snapshot periods, do we count those as separate detections? If we do it can cause heaping at a particular distance with the detection function.
> > > > >
> > > > > Scott
> > > > >

> > > > > > Hello,

> > > > > > Many, many thanks everyone!

> > > > > > On Saturday, June 13, 2020 at 12:50:36 AM UTC+10, Eric Howe wrote:
> > > > > > > Good day Scott,
> > > > > > > Re: activity period. Rowcliffe et al 2014 described methods for estimating the proportion of time active at camera height (and so available for detection by CTs), directly from times of detection, within any time interval (e.g. 24, 12, or 8 hours). There's an R package 'activity'. This can help you select daily Tk, and also account for temporally limited availability for detection within Tk.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Selection of t is a trade-off between missed observations of e.g. fast-moving animals close to the camera (missed if t is too large - no bias but costs you data), and data management (at some point, more observations of the same animals at almost the same location just creates more work measuring distances, without improving precision). Also, with smaller t, trigger speed and unavoidable delays between recordings could start to cause slight bias. Optimal values haven't been identified, and would likely vary across species and camera placements.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Eric H
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Thursday, 11 June 2020 20:03:23 UTC-4, scott Vogt wrote:
> > > > > > > > Thank you Eric,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Actually I should have said 12 hours for the activity period but will go over the data to see if there are any clear activity periods during the night. We get some day photos too but most are at night.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I'm not clear on how one selects the snapshot time, 3 seconds vs 5 seconds or whatever, what do you base this on?
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Understood on the camera viewing angle.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Again, many thanks.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Scott

> > > > > > > > On Thursday, June 11, 2020 at 7:28:53 PM UTC+10, Eric Rexstad wrote:
> > > > > > > > > Scott
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > A few more things to think about.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > You say your time period will be "night" therefore 8 hours; but which 8 hour period.  Defining the end points of the time period will be critical for animals with crepuscular activity patterns--moving the end points just a bit will alter the encounter rate.  Similarly recognise changing the time interval between snapshot moments will have an effect upon your effort, hence your estimates.  You'll need to be able to defend both decisions.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > The sampling fraction multiplier is viewing angle of camera divided by degrees (360) or radians (2*pi) in a complete circle.

> > > > > > > > > > This helps clarify things and in U.S. military parlance (I'm a civilian working for the military) I think I'm tracking now.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > We had 17 cameras set for 3 days and nights. Since most of the detections were in the night we would choose that as our time period. So 8 hours is 28,800 seconds. If we define our snap shot period as 3 seconds we would then have 9600 snapshot periods per camera. Correct? For the multiplier in the sampling fraction would then multiply that by the detection angle of the cameras we used for the sampling effort?
> > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > On Tuesday, June 9, 2020 at 2:36:42 AM UTC+10, Eric Howe wrote:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Good day Scott, and thanks Eric and Steve,
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Scott, regarding your question: "How are the snapshot moments defined/quantified": You define them as specific times of day. You also chose a daily time interval or intervals during which you will measure distances if animals are detected.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > It's helpful to plot detection times over the 24-hour day before measuring distances, because you might decide to reduce your daily survey duration to e.g. near dawn and dusk for crepuscular species or daylight hours for diurnal species (as in our article), and there's no need to measure distances to animals detected outside of this interval.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Also choose a value for t (duration of time step between snapshot moments). If t = 3, you could define moments as e.g. 0, 3, 6..., 57 seconds after the even minute, OR as 2, 5, 8,..., etc. seconds after the even minute, in real time. Moments are the same for all cameras. Regardless of when a camera is triggered, distances are measured only at these moments.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Tk is the total number of seconds a camera operates at location k. It's convenient to define a daily Tk, in seconds. This is the "time interval during which you will measure distances" above, so it might be less than the number of seconds in 24 hours; it might be the number of seconds within a 2- or 12-hour period. Multiply this by the number of days a camera operated and could have detected animals at a location to obtain Tk at that location. Then, dividing Tk by t (both in seconds) gives you the total number of opportunities to detect an animal at a location over the duration of a survey. This is your temporal effort at that location. Enter it as "Effort" in software IFF you are quantifying spatial effort < than a circle using a multiplier or the sampling_fraction argument. Alternatively, you can avoid multipliers and calculate Effort as described in the article (incorporating both spatial and temporal components)..
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Note that if we detected one animal at every opportunity, the encounter rate would be 1.0. In practice, encounter rates (detections per opportunity) are very low with camera trap point transects, because we observe no animals during most opportunities.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Hope this helps,
> > > > > > > > > > > Eric H

messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I agree with Olly's explanations. The graphic on imagur is worth 1000 words. Thanks.

I'll add that, regardless of how cameras are programmed, Tk (conveniently defined as daily Tk * sampling days, in seconds), divided by t (in seconds) should accurately quantify the number of opportunities in time to detect animals (and to measure distances) at point k. Whether or not we detect animals at those times depends on their location (distance from a CT).

Eric

On Tuesday, 14 July 2020 at 04:18:41 UTC-4 Olly Griffin wrote:
> Apologies, I just noticed an error in Photo Mode 2, correct below and also in this link if the image does not display correctly  https://imgur.com/a/8u63uIq.

> On Tuesday, 14 July 2020 at 15:10:32 UTC+7 Olly Griffin wrote:
> > Here's a little graphic I made to help illustrate the method to our team, perhaps it would be useful. Here, we pre-selected a t of 2 seconds, and with the snapshot falling on :00, :02, :04  etc of every minute. This shows the images or frames we would select under 4 different setups - one video, and 3 photo mode setups with different recovery times and burst modes (depending on camera model). Here, an animal enters the sensor FOV at 08:01:12.8 and remains in view for about 12 seconds. Each sensor triggers, and following a short delay (trigger time, dotted orange) begins to capture video or bursts of images. From this data, we select either video frames or photos (red lines) that are closest to the snapshot time (blue lines). For the video mode, a continuous video is captured for a defined length of time. For the photo modes, images are recorded with each firing of the sensor. This  shows why a short recovery time (between bursts) is required for CTDS. If the recovery time (a.k.a interval) was set to 15 seconds, the sensor would only fire once during the animal's time in the FOV. By setting the interval low, or using a higher number of images in each burst, a more continuous coverage of images is captured, allowing you to select images that are closest to the snapshot moments, and reducing bias. You can also see here how a single trigger event can produce more than one capture, if the burst continues over two snapshot moments (or includes images that are the closest to two snapshot moments, even if they don't fully overlap).
> >
> > On Monday, 13 July 2020 at 22:42:02 UTC+7 ej...@st-andrews.ac.uk wrote:
> > > Hi Scott,
> > >
> > > According to the original article, snapshot moments should be independent of triggering times, and predetermined as specific times of day. E.g. 0, 2, 4, ...., 58 seconds after the even minute for and interval (t ) = 2 seconds. In practice, we might look at our data after they had been collected and decide to set the interval to 1 or 3 or more seconds (to avoid missed detections, or unnecessary work), but we would still measure distances at those specific moments... Also, we would often measure distances to an animal or animals multiple times as it or they pass through the field of view (whenever it/they moves slowly enough to be present in the field of view during > 1 snapshot moment). We recommended programming cameras to record either video or long, rapid, bursts of still images, to ensure that some images would align (almost) perfectly with snapshot moments.
> > >
> > > I know there has been some discussion about how to collect data when cameras are not programmed to record e.g. video. With small t and cameras that can be triggered again immediately after recording an image, bias induced by the fact that observations of distance are not independent of trigger times should be slight. This approach would require small t  (not sure how small, but probably no longer than 2 seconds, and ideally shorter) so that observed distances would describe the animals' path through the zone of potential detection, not the location upon initial detection, which is expected to yield a positively biased distribution of observed distances. Multiple observations of distance to slow-moving animals would be recorded during a single pass through the zone of potential detection.
> > >
> > > Regarding your specific question, I think whether or not your 3 images would be recorded as one or as 2 or 3 observations depends on what t has been set to, and how far apart in time those 3 images are in time. E.g. if t = 2 and the images are 1 second apart, we would measure distances to animals in the first and third image. If t = 1 and the images are 2 seconds apart, we would miss detections at half of our snapshot moments, causing severe negative bias. You would only treat 3 images as one observation of distance if the time elapsed between images was much less than t.
> > >

Hello everyone

Thank you very much, this helps out a lot!

Scott

On Wednesday, July 15, 2020 at 3:26:04 AM UTC+10, ej...@st-andrews.ac.uk wrote:

> Hello,
> I agree with Olly's explanations. The graphic on imagur is worth 1000 words. Thanks.
>
> I'll add that, regardless of how cameras are programmed, Tk (conveniently defined as daily Tk * sampling days, in seconds), divided by t (in seconds) should accurately quantify the number of opportunities in time to detect animals (and to measure distances) at point k. Whether or not we detect animals at those times depends on their location (distance from a CT).
>
> Eric
>

> On Tuesday, 14 July 2020 at 04:18:41 UTC-4 Olly Griffin wrote:

> > Apologies, I just noticed an error in Photo Mode 2, correct below and also in this link if the image does not display correctly  https://imgur.com/a/8u63uIq.
> >
> >
> >

> > On Tuesday, 14 July 2020 at 15:10:32 UTC+7 Olly Griffin wrote:

> > > Here's a little graphic I made to help illustrate the method to our team, perhaps it would be useful. Here, we pre-selected a t of 2 seconds, and with the snapshot falling on :00, :02, :04  etc of every minute. This shows the images or frames we would select under 4 different setups - one video, and 3 photo mode setups with different recovery times and burst modes (depending on camera model). Here, an animal enters the sensor FOV at 08:01:12.8 and remains in view for about 12 seconds. Each sensor triggers, and following a short delay (trigger time, dotted orange) begins to capture video or bursts of images. From this data, we select either video frames or photos (red lines) that are closest to the snapshot time (blue lines). For the video mode, a continuous video is captured for a defined length of time. For the photo modes, images are recorded with each firing of the sensor. This  shows why a short recovery time (between bursts) is required for CTDS. If the recovery time (a.k.a interval) was set to 15 seconds, the sensor would only fire once during the animal's time in the FOV. By setting the interval low, or using a higher number of images in each burst, a more continuous coverage of images is captured, allowing you to select images that are closest to the snapshot moments, and reducing bias. You can also see here how a single trigger event can produce more than one capture, if the burst continues over two snapshot moments (or includes images that are the closest to two snapshot moments, even if they don't fully overlap).
> > >

> > > On Monday, 13 July 2020 at 22:42:02 UTC+7 ej...@st-andrews.ac.uk wrote:

> > > > Hi Scott,
> > > >
> > > > According to the original article, snapshot moments should be independent of triggering times, and predetermined as specific times of day. E.g. 0, 2, 4, ...., 58 seconds after the even minute for and interval (t ) = 2 seconds. In practice, we might look at our data after they had been collected and decide to set the interval to 1 or 3 or more seconds (to avoid missed detections, or unnecessary work), but we would still measure distances at those specific moments... Also, we would often measure distances to an animal or animals multiple times as it or they pass through the field of view (whenever it/they moves slowly enough to be present in the field of view during > 1 snapshot moment). We recommended programming cameras to record either video or long, rapid, bursts of still images, to ensure that some images would align (almost) perfectly with snapshot moments.
> > > >
> > > > I know there has been some discussion about how to collect data when cameras are not programmed to record e.g. video. With small t and cameras that can be triggered again immediately after recording an image, bias induced by the fact that observations of distance are not independent of trigger times should be slight. This approach would require small t  (not sure how small, but probably no longer than 2 seconds, and ideally shorter) so that observed distances would describe the animals' path through the zone of potential detection, not the location upon initial detection, which is expected to yield a positively biased distribution of observed distances. Multiple observations of distance to slow-moving animals would be recorded during a single pass through the zone of potential detection.
> > > >
> > > > Regarding your specific question, I think whether or not your 3 images would be recorded as one or as 2 or 3 observations depends on what t has been set to, and how far apart in time those 3 images are in time. E.g. if t = 2 and the images are 1 second apart, we would measure distances to animals in the first and third image. If t = 1 and the images are 2 seconds apart, we would miss detections at half of our snapshot moments, causing severe negative bias. You would only treat 3 images as one observation of distance if the time elapsed between images was much less than t.
> > > >
> > > > Eric H
> > > >
> > > > On Sunday, 12 July 2020 at 22:20:38 UTC-4 scott Vogt wrote:
> > > > > Hello Again,
> > > > >
> > > > > Have another question. I think I know the answer but want to make sure. If our cameras are set to take 3 images automatically when triggered, then those 3 frames are all within the same  snapshot moment and would be counted as one detection and distance, correct?
> > > > >
> > > > > Scott
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Friday, June 19, 2020 at 7:35:10 AM UTC+10, scott Vogt wrote:
> > > > > > Hello Eric,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > the substrate is limestone karst and is very rocky. I think the animals (deer and pigs) just move slowly because of that.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I've been putting the distance data into bins of varying sizes and that has helped. This helps the model fit but the density estimates are not all that different from the models with bad fit. Six deer were recognizable as individuals as were three pigs. Extrapolating the percentage of known to unknown animals for a population estimate and using known home ranges (gps collars) for estimating the area sampled produced a very similar density estimate for the deer and a lower estimate for the pigs but still in the ballpark.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The area is 35 ha and was just enclosed by fencing to keep out the deer and pigs. The area will be "de-ungulated" in the coming months so we'll be able to see how accurate the estimates are. The estimates do fit well with known densities elsewhere on Guam. One problem is that the cameras were in place before the fence was put up. Fence construction might have moved some animals off of the site. I don't think that happened but it's possible.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thank you very much everyone for all of the help!
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Scott
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Thursday, June 18, 2020 at 12:19:24 AM UTC+10, Eric Howe wrote:
> > > > > > > Good day Scott,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > As Eric and Steve mention, we accept and include non-independent observations. If its midpoint is visible, and the time is within Tk and during a snapshot moment, we record distance and include the observations. It doesn't cause cause bias because a single animal can only be detected once per location per snapshot moment.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > The issue with apparent heaping is potentially more complicated. Measuring distances to "resting" animals caused problems in simulations, because an animal that remains in front of the camera can contribute large numbers of observations, and if they are at moderate to far distances, decreasing functions may not fit the data well. Our (imperfect) solution was to avoid sampling during times when animals "rest".
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Animals that are awake and moving slightly (thus triggering the sensor) but not going anywhere could cause the same effect, and we don't have a clear reason to sensor the observations (the animal is "active").
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I would suggest checking the times of day when cameras detected these lingering animals, and see if they are similar. If there are specific times of day when animals are at their most mobile (e.g. crepuscular?), such that animals detected at these times pass by the camera (often contributing > 1, but not dozens or hundreds, of observations) rather than lingering in front of it, then you could limit Tk to these times. That could exclude most or all lingering animals from the data, improving fit without causing bias.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Bessone et al. (2020) sensored observations of animals obviously reacting to the camera, and this improved fit (another imperfect solution to a similar problem).   https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2664.13602.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > If you had only one animal that lingered in front of a camera and this animal created a "bump" in the observed distances far from 0, you could just say so and exclude the animal or most of the observations it contributed.

Dear Eric and Stephan

Thanks both for your quick and insightful responses! I will certainly try-out that vignette soon.

This is very interesting! So if we use the half-normal MCDS model we are basically doing the exact same thing as the fully stratified CDS (at least if there is 1 covariate which is the same as the strata).

In this case, I imagine the sample size should also be 60-80 for MCDS, and the 'dampening' effect that Eric mentioned on the dependence between estimates when pooling data across years, does not apply?

Thanks Eric for the warning on dependence between estimates when pooling data across years to assess temporal trends. I realize it is not ideal but we have insufficient sample sizes per year. Are there other strategies I could deploy to reduce the problem of dependence across years in addition to using MCDS?  For example, would you recommend to (1) pool data across all 5 survey years to make estimates per year, or (2) pool data from years that have the most similar detection functions, or (3) pool data from 2 subsequent survey years assuming they’d have more similar features, or (4) something else or none of the above J..?

Thanks again!

Mylo

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Full geographic stratification Vs.using stratum as a covariate ~ some mysterious results..
messages.body_plain:
Mylo, if you only need an overall abundance estimate, 60-80 would be good, whether you’re doing a stratified analysis or an MCDS analysis.  When you need good precision on individual stratum estimates, then you need more.  As far as I know, no-one has really looked into this.  Clearly, if some strata have very small sample sizes, estimation for those strata will be imprecise and potentially biased.  No reason why you shouldn’t pool data across years for fitting an MCDS model.  But bear in mind that for line transect sampling, usually the largest source of variation is in encounter rate, not in estimating the detection function, and pooling only benefits the latter, so I doubt that you would gain much.  You can check for your data whether encounter rate is the largest component of variance.

Steve

Dear Eric and Stephan

Thanks both for your quick and insightful responses! I will certainly try-out that vignette soon.

This is very interesting! So if we use the half-normal MCDS model we are basically doing the exact same thing as the fully stratified CDS (at least if there is 1 covariate which is the same as the strata).

In this case, I imagine the sample size should also be 60-80 for MCDS, and the 'dampening' effect that Eric mentioned on the dependence between estimates when pooling data across years, does not apply?

Thanks Eric for the warning on dependence between estimates when pooling data across years to assess temporal trends. I realize it is not ideal but we have insufficient sample sizes per year. Are there other strategies I could deploy to reduce the problem of dependence across years in addition to using MCDS?  For example, would you recommend to (1) pool data across all 5 survey years to make estimates per year, or (2) pool data from years that have the most similar detection functions, or (3) pool data from 2 subsequent survey years assuming they’d have more similar features, or (4) something else or none of the above J..?

Thanks again!

Mylo

messages.body_plain:
Hi listfolks,

Just to follow-up on this. Jez and I corresponded off-list to see what
was going on. It looks like the issue was that the covariate in the
detection function was a character variable, which was coerced into a
factor for fitting the detection function. Unfortunately it seems that
Distance/mrds doesn't currently save this conversion so when the
dsm.var.prop summary() function comes to look at the covariates it
doesn't know what to do with the factor.

Jez was able to solve this by refitting the detection function having
converted the character variable to factor (i.e., data$var <-
as.factor(data$var)) then refitting the dsm with this corrected
detection function.

I'll make some changes to mrds to get around this problem in future but
thought it was worth posting the work-around in case anyone else has
this issue.

cheers,
--dave

messages.subject: Justifying Left Truncation of Point Count Data
messages.subject_clean: Justifying Left Truncation of Point Count Data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have 20 years of distance sampling point-transect forest bird data that I have been analyzing with the ds() function.  I have determined from AIC analyses of models fitted to pooled (across years) data, that the detection function with Hazard Rate and Observer as covariate is the best model.  Therefore, I use that parameterization to model each year of data.  For most years, goodness of fit tests show that the models fit the data; however, I have one year where the data are unusual, with a very high number of birds detected at distance <= 5m.  This causes the model to fail a goodness of fit test.  I did not collect the data myself so it will be difficult for me to determine if the anomalous data are spurious or not.

So, my question is, would I be justified in left truncating data for this year in order to fit a model that passes a goodness of fit test?  I only need to truncate by 5 meters, but I do not left truncate for any other years.  On one hand it seems like it is cherry picking/data mining, while on the other hand it seems like a way to preserve an entire year worth of data; though perhaps this could produce an estimate that is biased high?  I've attached a plot of the model.

Best regards,

Leo

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Justifying Left Truncation of Point Count Data
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Justifying Left Truncation of Point Count Data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Leo and list,

Thanks for the question.  A few things:

- For point transect data, it is very hard to judge the fit (or where
lack of fit is coming from) by looking at the detection probability
plot, because the histogram bars in that plot are scaled to account for
the fact that the area associated with each distance bin increases with
increasing distance.  The first bin in your plot represents 0-2.5m, and
so an area of pi*2.5^2 = 19.63m^2.  The second bin is 2.5-5m, so an area
of pi*5^2 - pi*2.5^2 =  58.9m^2.  The third bin is 5-7.5m, so an area of
98.2m.  Notice that this area is going up linearly, by about 39m^2 with
each bin.  So, the farther from the line, the bigger the area
represented by each bin, and so the more animals we expect to detect if
detectability does not change.  Hence, in order to produce histograms
that match the estimated detection probability if the fit is good, the
histogram bars are scaled by dividing by the distance.  This means that
any lack of fit in the bins close to the point are exaggerated - often
this is only a few detections.  A better plot to look at for this
purpose is the probability density plot, which you can get from
plot(x, pdf = TRUE)
where x is the fitted object returned by ds()

- You mention that the model fails a goodness of fit test, and that you
attribute this to the <5m distances, but it could easily be that big
cluster of distances at 30m that is causing it -- this is lots more
detections than those at the closer distances for the reasons mentioned
above.  Have a look at the chi-square values you get from using the
ds.gof(x)
function.  There is a good example of exactly this in the example given
in the free online workshop Chapter 3
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter3/
in the "Case study" video lecture for chaffinch, where the detection
function appears to show lack of fit for close distances, but the bigger
contribution to lack-of-fit comes from bigger distances.  In that case,
the model does not fail the goodness-of-fit test, but the idea is similar.

- Even if you do have a few additional detections at low distances in
this one year, it it unlikely to bias the analysis, particularly if
you're fitting to multiple years of data -- you can see from your fitted
detection functions plot that you have "too many" detections at the
close distance and then "too few" at the slightly larger distances, but
that the estimated probability of detection balances these two.  You are
estimating that probability of detection is 1 out to about 30m for one
observer and 50m for another (the width of the "shoulder" - the flat
part of the detection function), which seems implausible to me for many
forest bird species, depending on how you detect them, etc -- so there
may be some other reason why the analysis is not working well.

- Given all of the above (and in the absence of further info), I see no
reason to left truncate this one year of data.  (On the other hand,
assuming you have a fairly large sample size, you'll probably find that
left truncation makes almost no difference to the result, because those
are only a very small number of detections.  All the same, no reason to
do it.)

- Lastly, I note that we very recently discovered a bug in the Distance
package associated with left truncation
(https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/Distance/issues/64 - the title
there is about camera trapping, but the bug was not due to the fact it's
camera trapping data, but due to the left truncation associated with
that analysis).  The bug is fixed, and the fix will be rolled out on an
up-coming release of the Distance package, due out by the end of the month.

I'll be happy to correspond with you off the list regarding your
analysis if that seems helpful and either you or I could post back to
the list with any additional insights.

Best wishes, Len Thomas

--

Deepti

It is possible that environmental factors that affect detectability may also influence encounter rates; so it is plausible to use the same covariate in both the detection function model and the dsm model.  I'm not certain, but I don't think there are serious consequences of this for either point or interval estimates of abundance.  Someone with first-hand experience with this might have thoughts.

I don't understand the second question.  Segments are not equivalent to samples.  If you have used 'Sample.Label' column, the function ds() understands this to be the transect on which the detections were made.  It is very common for there to be >1 detection on a transect; ds() handles this without a problem.

Are you trying to estimate abundance with dsm or with ds?

messages.subject: Three distance sampling workshops in Aug, Sept, Oct: registration now open
messages.subject_clean: Three distance sampling workshops in Aug, Sept, Oct: registration now open
messages.body_plain:
In August, September and October of 2020, the University of St Andrews continues its remote delivery of interactive distance sampling training workshops.  We are offering three workshops addressing:
mark-recapture distance sampling
spatial modelling of distance sampling data
introductory distance sampling

Registration for all workshops is currently open, but closing date for the August workshop is fast approaching (see below).

Description of each workshop, in chronological order, found below along with URLs for registration and additional information.

Mark recapture distance sampling training workshop 24th and 25th August 2020 17:00-19:30 British Summer Time

Registration is now open for our training workshop on mark-recapture distance sampling.  Join us by video from anywhere around the world!  For full details, and to register, please go to

https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/mark-recapture-distance-sampling-workshop/

Workshop Overview

Conventional distance sampling methods assume that all animals at zero distance are detected with certainty.  However, in some situations this assumption is violated, and some animals are missed, causing a negative bias in the density and abundance estimates.  This occurs on some shipboard surveys of marine mammals, for example, where animals may be missed on the trackline because they are underwater while the survey vessel passes, or because the sea conditions are rough so that even some animals right on the line are missed.  The former (being underwater and so not available for detection) is often called availability bias and the latter perception bias.  This methodology is particularly suited for investigations of cetaceans and other marine mammals.

In this two-day workshop, we cover survey protocols and analytical methods for dealing with both perception bias and availability bias. The workshop is intended for those already familiar with the basics of distance sampling.

Instructors: Len Thomas and David Borchers

Timing

24th and 25th August 2020

17:00-19:30 British Summer Time // 12:00-14:30 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT) // 09:00-11:30 Pacific Daylight Time (PDT)

Enrolment limit

15 participants; registration deadline 31 July

Format and delivery method

The workshop will be a mix of live online interactive sessions, delivered via videoconference software (Microsoft Teams), and computer exercises. There will be two sessions on successive days, with a total class time of 4 hours (including breaks) and an additional computer exercise to complete after the first day and before the second.   Exercises can be undertaken using Distance for Windows or R (via the mrds package).

Spatially explicit models for distance sampling data: density surface modelling in practice 5-9 October 2020

5-9 October 2020, 1700-1900 BST // 1200-1400 EDT // 0900-1100 PDT

This course will cover how to fit spatial models to distance sampling data ("density surface modelling") in R. This will include:
Brief overview of distance sampling
Generalized additive models
Fitting, checking and selecting density surface models
Predicting abundance
Making maps
Examples will be based around a line transect survey of sperm whales in the western Atlantic.

For full details and to register, visit

https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/spatial-modelling-live-online-workshop-2/

Instructor: David Miller

Format:

The course will consist of 5 live sessions delivered over videoconference. Between these sessions there will be practical R exercises to complete and to assist with these practicals there will be text-based "office hours", where participants questions can be addressed. Each videoconference session will include time for lecturing and discussion of practical exercises.

Enrolment limit:

15 participants; registration deadline 05 September

Prerequisites:

You should already know about distance sampling, for example by having taken an introductory workshop in person or online (either interactively or via our free pre-recorded lectures). You should also have some basic R knowledge. Prior to the course we will running a software test meeting to ensure everyone can participate satisfactorily.

Please contact David Miller (dl...@st-andrews.ac.uk) with questions regarding the spatial modelling workshop.

Introductory distance sampling 07-18 September or 21 September - 02 October 2020

Fundamental principles of distance sampling, from the perspective of survey design, field protocol for data gathering and analysis of distance sampling data.

For full details, and to register, please go to

https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/distance-live-online-workshops/

Instructor: Eric Rexstad

The 21 Sept-02 Oct offering of the workshop is being delivered in the morning UK time (0900-1130) such that participants from east Asia, Australia and New Zealand as well as Europeans can take part, while the 07-18 September workshop will be delivered early evening UK time (1700-1930) for attendees in Europe and the Americas to participate.

Format:

Ten sessions spread across two working weeks.  Combination of lectures and practical exercises along with interactive polls.

Enrolment limit:  15 participants for each of the two workshops

Registration closing dates: 14 August (for first workshop), 21 August (for second workshop)

Please contact Eric Rexstad (eric.r...@st-andrews.ac.uk) with questions regarding the introductory workshop.
--
Eric Rexstad

I have the following table:

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Species richness and distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Delphine

Distance sampling is a method of estimating species abundance or density, so it is not used to directly measure species richness.  But there have been a few papers that try to incorporate elements of distance sampling, particularly issues surrounding rare species.  Here is a smattering of literature:
Buckland, S. T., Baillie, S., Dick, J., Elston, D., Magurran, A., Scott, M., Smith, R., Somerfield, P., Studeny, A. C., & Watt, A. (2012). How should regional biodiversity be monitored? Environmental and Ecological Statistics, 19(4), 601-626. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10651-012-0202-7

Buckland, S. T., Studeny, A. C., Magurran, A., & Newson, S. (2010). Biodiversity monitoring: the relevance of detectability. In A. Magurran, & B. McGill (Eds.), Biological Diversity: Frontiers in Measurement and Assessment (pp. 25-36). Oxford University Press.

Buckland, S. T. (2009). Quantifying biodiversity. Significance, 6(3), 105-107. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1740-9713.2009.00371.x

Roberts TE, Bridge TC, Caley MJ, Baird AH (2016) The Point Count Transect Method for Estimates of Biodiversity on Coral Reefs: Improving the Sampling of Rare Species. PLoS ONE 11(3): e0152335. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0152335
Yamaura, Y., and Royle, J. A.. 2017. Community distance sampling models allowing for imperfect detection and temporary emigration. Ecosphere 8( 12):e02028. 10.1002/ecs2.2028 <https://doi.org/10.1002/ecs2.2028>

messages.body_plain:
Delphine

Thanks for your report about problems with `dht2`.  We'll have a look at the problem and may contact you off-line about particulars.

Meanwhile, you should be able to work around the problem in the manner you described: replace the two columns distbegin and distend with a single column named "distance", into that column place the midpoint of the bin (e.g. below your end points are 0.08 and 0.18, use the value 0.13 for distance.

Then use the "cutpoints=" argument in your call to ds() to conduct your binned analysis.  You should be able to send the result of that call to ds() off to dht2().  Let us know if that works for you.

messages.body_plain:
Hello & Thank you Eric and Delphine. But when it comes to multispecies DS survey with binned distance (e.g. songbird by point or seabirds by transect), would it make sense to estimate local guild species richness in a DS framework, as one can expect to detect all species in the closest bin but less so in the further bins? Would it be theoretically “allowed” ??? Of course, assuming models would converge, regional size estimates would make no sense but DSM application could be partially interesting by outputting a layer of local sp richness, no?

Sorry if I am totally misleading but curiosity nibbles me (as we say in French)

Thanks a lot for all the so fast replies to any questions almost everyday on this list!

Pierre

Hi again

I am conducting analysis on line transect data from a stratified study region (2 PAs), one species, two survey years. I require abundance estimates per region and per year (and I know there are some problems with regards to pooling multiple years).

I have found the model of my dreams for this species: it is a HR key function with PA as covariate. With this model I have produced abundance and density estimates per strata (the 4 possible year-pa combinations), but when I produce a summary() or print() of the ds object the variance are different compared to when I use dht2(). I think this may have something to do with the settings for "varn" of dht2 but when I try different options, there is still quite a big difference in CV and SE.

So my questions are:

1.) Why does this difference exists (how are the variances calculated differently between the ds() and dht2() functions?

2.) Which one to use?

3.) Or should I forget about this alltogether and give bootstrapping a go?

Thanks so much in advance!

Mylo
