messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Variance estimates with ds() versus dht2()
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Variance estimates with ds() versus dht2()
messages.body_plain:
Mylo

There are lots of combinations governing variance estimation with the two functions in the package.  Recognise also that ds() is actually calling the function dht() for abundance estimation.  You've not specified where the differences in variances are manifested: at the stratum level or the global level.

The function dht2() is used when there is non-standard kinds of stratification and an overall estimate for the entire study area required different types of weighted averages.

I think in your situation (where you are not interested in study area-wide estimates, just the year/stratum-specific estimates), you can rely upon the computations carried out by ds() (via dht()).  Correct me if I'm wrong about my assumptions.

If you want some detail on the variance calculations used by dht2(), have a look at this diagram

https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-mult/strat.pdf

messages.subject: Using dssd survey design for small r point transects/camera trap distance sampling
messages.subject_clean: Using dssd survey design for small r point transects/camera trap distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, a question relating to assessing survey coverage for point transects with a low radius...

I have used the dssd package in R to distribute points within a study area for a camera trap distance sampling survey (although this would apply to any point counts with a low survey radius (e.g. species who's call don't carry far)). I used 260 samplers, with a 45 degree grid rotation (to avoid edge effects along the common horizontal edges of this study area). Eyeballing the grid, it looks good, with good coverage (Samplers.png)

As this is a camera trap survey, the truncation value is low - around 30m (in this example, I used 20m, but the principle is the same). Using a 1000-point coverage grid to assess coverage, the results indicate poor coverage (Coverage.png). I think this is due to the low radius/truncation distance - most of the coverage points fall outside of the surveyed area (i.e. outside of the 20m radius from each sampler). The occasional high coverage score is likely just a coverage point landing within a sampler radius.

The densities of samplers in this case is pretty standard for camera trapping (around 2.8km between samplers), and even increasing the density would not have a significant effect on total area covered, given the low radius/truncation distance.

So in this case, I think using the dssd grid point based coverage is inappropriate. Is there a more suitable method for assessing coverage in this case? I'm fairly happy to move on with the design without a formal assessment of coverage, as by its nature a systematic grid of points will have good coverage - but it would be interesting to check for subtle edge effects.

Thanks in advance for any advice.

Olly

messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric

Many thanks for your quick response!

The differences are manifested both at the stratum and global level, although the difference in global level is much smaller (difference in CV is 0.02 for global versus 0.14-0.17 for stratum-level). Since the variance is much lower for dht2() compared to ds(), I’d prefer to use dht2(), and as the results are stratified, it does seem a correct approach.. However, I obviously don’t want to go for an increase in precision at the cost of accuracy. Given the added detail, do you still think ds() is better for this particular analysis? If so, can the proportions of variance contribution (df, encounter rate, cluster size), also be calculated using df?

I failed to mention that in addition to the stratum specific estimates (year/PA), I am also interested in obtaining a study-area wide estimate for each year (i.e. combined PA, singular year).

Following your cheat sheet, as well as your recommendations in this conversation: https://groups.google.com/g/distance-sampling/c/BAhQmzts9nI/m/cBA-2ndyAwAJ

I use the following code for stratum-specific estimates:
dht2(BAN_16_20_HR_PA_T79, flatfile=BAN_16_20, strat_formula= ~Region.Label, convert_units = conversion.factor,
                     er_est = c("O1"), multipliers = NULL,sample_fraction = 1, ci_width = 0.95, stratification="geographical")

(where region.label is either of the 4 year/PA combinations). My example is actually a hybrid between geographical and effort_sum stratification. I checked and effort_sum did produce the same stratum-level results (with the difference being in total versus average abundance estimate & variance for the pooled global estimate).

Then, for the combined PA per Year estimate, I take a ‘production line’ approach, by merging the Region.Label in to 2 categories and adjusting the total area (summed of 2 PAs). And then using the same code as above. I am not sure if this is an entirely correct approach? It does yield an abundance estimate that is roughly the sum of the above, but it does not account for the different area size or effort for both PAs (which is relatively minor: 1,670 versus 1,736 sq. km area, and 1.391 versus 1,368km effort).

I also tried strat_formula= ~YEAR, but that keeps coming with an error message:

>1 Area defined for a single stratum label, check data

 Would you have a recommendation on how to approach the combined PA/per year estimate?

I gave the bootdht function a go as well, but it only produces results for the global estimate. Perhaps I shouldn’t add even more options then we already have!

Thanks again so much for your advice!

Mylo

messages.body_plain:
Mylo

dht() (called by ds()) handles geographic stratification just fine, so no particular need to use dht2() when stratification is present.  The untidy bit of your analysis is that as you note, you're defining strata using a combination of space and time.  I don't actually know what is correct in this situation.

dht() does not have the added code to produce the variance component calculation you request, but it is a pretty straightforward calculation that could be done manually (see below)

A possible partial explanation for your difference in CVs among your various analytical combinations is the use of the O1 option for encounter rate variance; I don't believe we've tested that option. What was your motivation for choosing that encounter rate variance calculation? It should be used when there are gradients in line length along with gradients in animal density; your ds() analysis cannot directly access the equivalent option  when calling dht().

Given the bespoke nature of your analysis, my suggestion for your region-wide annual estimates would be to use the "stratum" specific estimates from your 4 year/stratum estimates and their measures of precision; manually combine them in the manner shown in the cheat-sheet from yesterday for geographic stratification.  I appreciate it's not elegant, but we don't have code that handles your specific situation.

messages.body_plain:
Olly

On the whole, I have to agree with your assessment.  As you note in your penultimate paragraph, setting software aside, deploying a set of 260 circles in a systematic fashion across a polygon is likely to produce reasonably uniform coverage across the polygon; implying that all points within the polygon are approximately equally likely to receive coverage by samplers.

As your tabular output demonstrates, the 260 cameras (assuming 360 field of view) will "see" 0.02% of your 1620 km^2.  Although small, the salient idea is whether all points within the study area are equally likely to be sampled.  If you were obsessive about looking for edge effects, I suspect your coverage grid need a much finer mesh (and associated increase in computation time).

Short answer to your question in bold:  I don't think so.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks again Eric

It sounds the dht() (called by ds()) is the tried and tested solution, so I’ll move ahead with that. In case anyone is interested in delving deeper in the dht2 variance mystery: I used all different possible varn options for line transects (R2,3,4, S1, and O1,02,03), and the variances produced were near-similar whilst all very different to that of dht(). I chose O1 as it is described as “systematic line placement, post-stratification with overlapping strata (akin to S1)”, and my data for different years overlaps in space.

Moving on and ahead: Following your solution on the region-wide estimate, summing all 4 year/stratum estimates would not give me the desirable 2PA for 1 year, but rather 2PA summed for both years. If I use the 2 year/stratum estimates within the desired year then following the geographic stratification would be easy (just summing), but would it not ignore the variance caused by using a pooled DF for 2 years? I wouldn’t want to use the effort-weighted sum either as it gives an average over the 2 years and 2 areas.

I promise that was my final variance question J thanks again!

Milou

messages.subject: Re: AIC:NA in dsm model with Family quasi poisson
messages.subject_clean: AIC:NA in dsm model with Family quasi poisson
messages.body_plain:
Thank you Eric and Mikhail for the help.

This is to update on this issue. I went through more literature and figure out a manual way to calculate AIC for quasi-poisson models:

mod_ndvi <- dsm(count ~ s(ndvi), hn.modCos$ddf, segdata, obsdata, engine = "gam")

#LOG LIKELIHOOD of mod_ndvi

LL <- logLik(mod_ndvi)

#MODEL DF = no. of parameters (p) = sum of smooth (edf) + parametric (nsdf) terms

p <- sum(mod_ndvi$edf) + sum(b$nsdf)

AIC <- 2*p - 2*LL

I have validated the above formula with those models which were calculating default AIC and found it correct. This is helpful if I want to compare models using different family objects.

Apart from this, calculating c-hat value (overdispersion parameter) helped in model selection.

Now, I am confused with QQ plot of quasi-poisson, negative-binomial and Tweedie family.

--QQ plot of quasi-poisson family shows points away from line while other two seems to do fine. Other model parameters (test statistics, p-values, deviance explained, residual vs predictor variable etc.) are better in case of quasi-poisson model. Would it be a good idea to reject a quasi-poisson model just based on QQ plot and select other family objects??

Also,
--I find concurvity between spatial variable and habitat variable is >0.8. How serious is this for a model? Should I drop one of the variables??

Thanks again.

Deepti Gupta

>
> Results and model fit is coming as expected.
>
> I am trying to get the AIC value for this model using the following code:
>
> AIC(mod_ndvi)
>
> It shows 'NA' in the results.
>
> While I run the same code for a model with the family object: Tweedie, AIC shows up!
>
> Am I missing something with the family object quasi Poisson??
>
> PS: I was going through some literature that suggests quasi Poisson distribution is best suited for GLM regression. Would you please suggest some readings (with fewer technicalities) to understand the concept behind family objects?

> Regards
> Deepti

messages.body_plain:
Deepti, just a brief comment on the quasi-Poisson.  You need to bear in mind that there is no such distribution as the quasi-Poisson.  Instead, the Poisson model is assumed, then a dispersion parameter is estimated, to inflate the variance from the Poisson.  So if you need to resort to quasi-Poisson, it is because the Poisson is a poor fit to your data, so departure from the line in the QQ plot for Poisson is perhaps to be expected.  By contrast, the negative binomial and Tweedie distributions can have variance greater than the mean, so should fit better.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] population density - cryptic species
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] population density - cryptic species
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cicero,

I don't think an R package will do much to improve matters for you. The most basic assumption of Distance analysis is that detection probability is at least close to 100% in the nearest distance band. If you detect lower densities in near bands than in further ones, but can reasonably argue that this is due to individuals avoiding the transect by moving into adjacent (but still relatively close) distance bands, such that detection of birds up to the band in which you saw them approaches 100%, you can get around this by amalgamating distance bands up to the band with the highest density of observations, so that detectability decreases with distance as one would expect. However, if your closest detections are at 100m, for a bird like tinamou in forest habitat, I strongly suspect that this is NOT an assumption you can reasonably make. Between your transect and 100m, I would have thought there could be many tinamou that you aren't detecting. In this situation, I think a robust distance analysis seems like an unlikely prospect, unless you can think of a more innovative approach using camera traps, passive detection by call (whether directly or from recordings - though you would potentially have to distinguish individuals, and also make an assessment of the proportion of individuals calling), or response to playback.

Might be that others have ideas about how to make a traditional distance approach work - I will wait and see what the more knowledgeable contributors to this forum say!

Cheers,

Mark
